```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The question asks for a paying customer within 90 days. B names a specific prospective buyer: a Wisconsin public adjuster and its affiliated roofing contractor. A names no customer, only a generic eng-manager persona.",
    "B's willingness-to-pay evidence is sourced and directly comparable. Five vendors charge $65–$250/mo to the same buyer type, which supports a $99–$250/mo price for a single firm. A's price anchor is undercut by Slack Code, which the brief says ships free inside every Slack plan and sets a $0 reference price for the core feature.",
    "Both niches are crowded. But B's competitors are small vertical vendors at similar price points. A's competitors include an incumbent with massive distribution plus a free open-source option, which makes winning the first sale harder for a solo builder.",
    "A's key feasibility claims are marked [unsourced] and so count as missing: that a solo builder can ship it in six weeks, and that demand extends beyond engineering. The brief also says the likely purchase driver is SOC2, SSO, and governance depth that a solo build is unlikely to match.",
    "B's scope is bounded: intake plus document extraction for one known customer. It has real compliance work (Wisconsin's Insurance Data Security Law, breach-notification rules), but that is scoped to one buyer. A's security bar must satisfy enterprise engineering teams before adoption."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence is two blog quotes. One is an operations lead who cannot see what agents produced; that is a visibility and reporting complaint, not a request for jointly steering and handing off agent tasks. The other complains that Slack is a poor place for execution traces. Neither shows anyone paying or willing to pay for a standalone multiplayer workspace. The main 'signal' left is inference from competitors converging on the same features, plus a YC Fall 2026 RFS mention with no link.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. B's edge rests mostly on the named customer pair, and the brief itself lists 'Is the named customer's commitment real/recurring or informal?' as an open question. If that commitment is informal, B's advantage shrinks a lot. B's market is also tiny (188 licensed PAs in Wisconsin), its demand quotes come from a Florida firm and a Reddit post rather than the named customer, and its compliance burden is real. B is the better first bet for one paying customer in 90 days, not necessarily the better long-term business."
}
```
